performers: Roxana Pavel Goldstein, violin; Constance Schoepflin, flute; Matthew Ganong, harpsichord; Advent Chamber Orchestra
question: How can the keyboard accompany a dialogue and also answer it?
intro: The concerto contracts to its three soloists: flute, violin and harpsichord. A short dotted figure passes between them while the keyboard alternates an accompanying bass with an independent upper voice.

sections.label: Opening exchanges · B minor and D major
sections.mNote: short refrains alternate with keyboard-led replies

cues.title: Three players remain
cues.text: The ripieno strings are silent throughout this movement. Flute and violin exchange a short dotted figure over the harpsichord’s bass; the keyboard can then turn from accompaniment to an answering melodic voice.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft full score, printed pp. 149–151, has only Flauto traverso, Violino principale and Cembalo. The opening violin figure is answered by the flute; this is an account of the opening passage, not an aligned entrance.

cues.title: A dotted figure travels
cues.text: Throughout the movement, follow the short long–short figure rather than assigning one permanent melody to one instrument. Its rhythm helps identify a reply even when the register, player and harmony change.
cues.evidence: The dotted opening figure recurs in the three upper parts across the printed score. No particular handover is assigned to this timestamp.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Six concertos presented together
cues.text: Bach dated the presentation score of the six Brandenburg Concertos 24 March 1721. Their dedicatee, Christian Ludwig of Brandenburg, received a collection with a different instrumental combination in each concerto, not six repetitions of one orchestral plan.
cues.evidence: The dedication date, dedicatee and differing scorings are documented in the surviving presentation score; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandenburg_Concerto_No._5 and the Bach-Gesellschaft score.

cues.title: The keyboard can answer
cues.text: Across the quieter replies, listen for an upper keyboard line as well as the bass. Bach writes out those melodic passages; the harpsichord is not confined to filling in chords underneath the other two soloists.
cues.evidence: The score alternates figured-bass accompaniment with a written-out right-hand part. Relative level is lower around 1:35–2:00, but the analysis cannot isolate the keyboard; no individual entrance is claimed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Refrain in another minor
cues.text: The middle exchanges carry the familiar dotted material into F♯ minor. The change is harmonic rather than a replacement of the instrumental group: the same three players continue their alternating phrases.
cues.evidence: The score places the third four-bar refrain in F♯ minor around bars 20–23. The report has a boundary at 2:24 and a sustained F♯-minor region around 2:15–2:45. The 2:20 map point is approximate, not bar-aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bach also played violin
cues.text: In 1703 Bach spent about half a year as a violinist in Duke Johann Ernst III’s private orchestra at Weimar. His later reputation as an organist can obscure this early experience inside an instrumental ensemble.

cues.title: Recognise rhythm through harmony
cues.text: As the later major-key refrain approaches, keep the opening rhythm in mind. A familiar figure can preserve the movement’s identity while a different bass changes its harmonic setting.
cues.evidence: The score’s fourth refrain lies in G major around bars 30–33. The report marks a boundary at 3:36 and a G-major region around 3:50–4:00; this note prepares a broad passage rather than announcing an exact chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Court musician before cantor
cues.text: Bach entered Prince Leopold’s service at Köthen in 1717 and moved to Leipzig in 1723. The Brandenburg dedication belongs to the court years; Leipzig would add the regular preparation of church cantatas to his duties.
cues.evidence: Bach-Archiv Leipzig chronology, 1717 and 1723; the 1721 dedication is preserved with the concertos.

cues.title: Bass beneath the ornaments
cues.text: In the longer keyboard replies, try following the bass independently of the decorated upper line. A held or repeated harmonic foundation can make several moving notes sound like an extension of one thought rather than several new phrases.
cues.evidence: The final episode has an independent written keyboard line above the bass. This is a passage-level listening suggestion; no machine-generated chord or exact ornamental note is identified.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The opening finds home
cues.text: The closing refrain restores the opening’s B minor and its paired flute-and-violin exchange. The keyboard returns to its accompanying role, so the ending recalls not just a tune but the original distribution of work between the players.
cues.evidence: The final four-bar refrain begins near bar 45 in the BGA score, printed p. 151. The report strengthens around 5:20–5:30, with B-minor estimates through the closing passage. The 5:18 placement is an estimate from score proportions and this late rise.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A cadence then resonance
cues.text: The final phrase settles and the recorded sound falls away. Leave room for the decay after the cadence: the next movement restores the ensemble, but no new instrument joins this ending.
cues.evidence: The report falls from −15.7 dB at 5:40 to −25.8 dB at 5:45 and below −70 dB at 5:50. The score ends with the same three instruments; the report does not locate the precise release.

transitions.title: Familiar figures change their harmonic ground
transitions.how: The keyboard-led episode carries the dotted figure away from the opening’s B minor and its relative major. The next refrain settles in F♯ minor, the minor dominant region. Flute and violin recover the compact paired statement while the harpsichord supports it from below. The change of key therefore preserves the phrase’s rhythm and the movement’s three-player scale rather than introducing a new theme or a larger ensemble.
transitions.evidence: BGA score, pp. 149–150, third refrain around bars 20–23; report boundary 2:24, higher level at 2:20–2:35 and F♯-minor estimates across 2:15–2:45. The nominal join is approximate.

transitions.title: The refrain opens into G major
transitions.how: A further keyboard episode leads towards the fourth refrain, now in G major. The flute and violin take up related material over the keyboard bass, but the refrain is varied rather than simply shifted note for note. The same dotted rhythm makes the connection audible while the major-key harmony changes its setting. An extended keyboard-led reply follows before the final return to B minor.
transitions.evidence: The score’s fourth refrain occupies approximately bars 30–33; its G-major setting and varied material are described in the movement’s structural account at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandenburg_Concerto_No._5. The report boundary at 3:36 precedes G-major estimates around 3:50–4:00; placement remains passage-level.

transitions.title: The keyboard yields the opening back
transitions.how: The final keyboard reply prepares B minor and gives way to the opening refrain in its original key. Violin and flute recover their close exchange above the bass while the harpsichord’s independent upper melody withdraws into accompaniment. This is a return of texture as well as pitch: the movement closes within the same three-instrument conversation in which it began.
transitions.evidence: BGA printed p. 151, final system, restores the opening statement before the closing cadence. The 5:18 estimate is supported by the recorded rise around 5:20 and the closing B-minor region, not by voice separation or exact bar alignment.

timeline.note: Violin and flute exchange the dotted figure above the keyboard bass; keyboard-led replies intervene.
The F♯-minor refrain and its reply pass the foreground between flute and the keyboard’s written upper part.
A G-major refrain leads into the final extended keyboard reply; violin and flute punctuate the dialogue.
The opening exchange returns in B minor, with the harpsichord accompanying beneath it.

composer.epithet: An organist, teacher and church musician who made a bass line, a dance rhythm and a fugue subject carry the same argument.
facts: Family musicians in Eisenach and Ohrdruf; school at Lüneburg; study of German, French and Italian scores
Arnstadt · Mühlhausen · Weimar · Köthen · Thomaskantor in Leipzig, 1723–50
Organ, harpsichord, clavichord and violin; an examiner of organs and a teacher of keyboard players
Cantatas, Passions, the B minor Mass, organ and keyboard cycles, concertos, unaccompanied string music
composer.background:
Bach was born into a family of professional musicians in Eisenach, where his father Johann Ambrosius served as a town musician. The surname already meant a trade: relatives supplied organists, cantors and instrumentalists across Thuringia. His mother died in 1694 and his father in 1695; at ten he went to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist in Ohrdruf who had studied with Pachelbel. Keyboard instruction belonged to that household, alongside school and choir. In 1700 Bach travelled to Lüneburg, where a place in the choir of St Michael’s school gave a boy without substantial means access to an education and a musical library.

The early career was practical and local. After a brief appointment at Weimar, he became organist of the New Church in Arnstadt in 1703, with a recently built instrument to test and play. His duties included working with students, and the town’s records preserve disputes over both his behaviour and his music. In 1705 he obtained leave to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck and stayed away much longer than authorised. Buxtehude’s organ works offered a model in which free passagework, recurring basses and strict counterpoint could occupy the same piece. Bach’s own organ preludes would retain that alternation between improvisatory display and composed argument.
